newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai baht two-tier system unlikely to see year-end.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht two-tier system unlikely to see year-end.

text.p: The Thai baht's two-tier trading system will not likely see the year-end, but it will remain in place as long as the Bank of Thailand (BOT) needs to intervene to defend the baht, according to a Reuters poll of 13 market analysts on Friday.
"How long the two-tier system will remain in place would depend on the need for the central bank to intervene in the future," said Charl Kengchon of the Thai Farmers Research Institute.
"The two-tier system is only a mechanism to boost the effectiveness of intervention," he added.
But of the 13 experts surveyed in Singapore and Bangkok 11 thought the system would remain in place only for another six months or less, with five of those expecting it to evaporate around August.
Charl Kengchon said it would last as long as the BOT needed to intervene and one said it may be made permanent.
But the consensus was that around August the market could start looking towards an end of the two-tier system.
This is because the BOT will want to wait for the maturity of forward long dollar/short baht positions, which were taken out during the mid-May speculative attack.
Analysts said a good portion of these speculative positions would be three month forwards, so would mature in August, and six month contracts would make up the vast bulk of the rest.

"There is talk out there in the market that some of the hedge funds may have already squared some of their deals but I think they (the Thai authorities) will wait at least until August," said Andrew Dermot Fung, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
"I would be very surprised if it were still in place in six months time," he added.

Also, Thailand has sought technical assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and while this has not developed into actual money assistance, were Thailand to ask for it the IMF would not be happy with a two-tier system.
"If Thailand did ask for actual help, the IMF would want some assurance that the two-tier system was on the way out," said one analyst at a European bank here.

It is important for Thailand to look to ending the two-tier system as with a widening current account deficit -- Thailand's current account deficit jumped to 112.3 billion baht in May from 15.5 billion in April -- it needs capital inflow.

For this to happen investor confidence must return and harsh capital controls do nothing to inspire confidence, although the Thai stock market shot up from eight-year lows after this week's adoption of a managed float system for the baht.

But Thailand needs more long-term capital inflows as overseas cash in the stock market is too transitory, analysts said. "They can keep some kind of capital controls but under a more structured framework and less ad hoc than it has been up to now," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.
"Investors have to be sure they are not going to change the rules on them. As it is right now, coming up with different rules every two or three weeks, is going to put people off for sure," he added.
